title: AI-Enhanced Structured Literacy Intervention for Secondary Students: A Case Study of Science of Reading
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an AI-powered literacy tool, Lexia PowerUp, can support reading growth among secondary students with significant reading difficulties. The study focuses on sixth-grade students receiving Tier 3 reading intervention and asks whether the program improves reading proficiency, how students progress across Word Study, Grammar, and Comprehension strands, and how usage relates to growth.

The intervention combined 50 minutes of daily Tier 3 reading support in a separate classroom with individualized use of Lexia PowerUp, an adaptive AI-enhanced literacy program for grades 6-12. Researchers tracked student outcomes using beginning-of-year and mid-year Achieve 3000 Lexile scores, along with Lexia placement and progress data collected from October 8, 2024 to April 1, 2025. The program also triggered teacher-led one-on-one support when students struggled repeatedly on specific sub-skills.

Participants were seven sixth-grade students in Virginia, USA, all identified for intensive reading intervention. The sample included six boys and one girl; five African American and two Caucasian students; all qualified for free or reduced lunch, and none had an IEP. The intervention occurred in a separate classroom setting and blended teacher-led small-group instruction with individualized AI-supported literacy practice.

Findings showed that all students improved their Lexile scores over the study period and made gains across Lexia strands, with some movement from foundational to intermediate levels in Word Study and Comprehension. However, all students remained below sixth-grade benchmarks, no students reached the advanced zone, and Grammar progress was especially limited. The authors conclude that AI-enhanced structured literacy may be a useful supplement to teacher-led intervention for struggling secondary readers, but results are preliminary and continued intensive support is needed.

identified_tools.name: Lexia PowerUp
identified_tools.description: An adaptive literacy intervention program for students in grades 6-12 that assesses reading skills and personalizes instruction across Word Study, Grammar, and Comprehension through interactive activities, scaffolding, and immediate feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within a Tier 3 reading intervention for sixth-grade struggling readers (n=7) for about six months. Students received daily intervention that combined small-group teacher-led instruction with individualized use of Lexia PowerUp. Outcomes were tracked with Achieve3000 Lexile assessments and Lexia PowerUp progress data. The study had no control group, so findings reflect the combined intervention context rather than Lexia PowerUp alone.

findings.finding_summary: All seven participants improved on Achieve3000 Lexile levels from the beginning to the middle of the school year, although all remained below the sixth-grade benchmark ranges reported in the paper. The authors noted that assessment administration conditions differed across time points, which may affect interpretation.

Lexia PowerUp progress data indicated movement from more foundational to more intermediate placement levels in Word Study and Comprehension, while Grammar showed little or no comparable advancement. No students reached the advanced zone in any strand.
findings.measure: Lexia PowerUp placement/progression zone across Word Study, Grammar, and Comprehension

findings.finding_summary: All students showed gains in Lexia PowerUp units across Word Study, Grammar, and Comprehension, though progress varied substantially by student and strand.
findings.measure: Units gained in Lexia PowerUp Word Study, Grammar, and Comprehension strands

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small case study without a control group or random assignment, relying on pre-post observational evidence from seven students at one site. The methodology is clearly described and peer reviewed, but causal claims are limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports modest positive pre-post gains in Lexile scores and strand progression, but impact is unclear because there is no comparison group and no reported effect size. Students improved yet remained substantially below grade-level benchmarks.
